x.A: More read replicas help read scaling, but they don't shorten the writer failover or keep connections alive during it.
x.B: A secondary cluster in the same Region needs the application to be updated on failover and keeps data synchronization as a separate job. It's more effort.
x.C: Memcached is a cache and doesn't keep write connections alive or shorten a failover.
x.D: RDS Proxy keeps the application's connections open and routes them to the new writer after failover, which reduces the downtime a failover causes, with only an endpoint change.

x.A: An Auto Scaling group can't span Regions, so it can't be extended into AZs in a second Region.
x.B: A cross-Region Aurora Replica works, but an Aurora global database is the better-managed option, with lower replication lag and faster recovery.
x.C: DMS replication has more lag and operational work, and it's not the most fault-tolerant option.
x.D: Deploying the web and application tiers in a second Region, an Aurora global database across the Regions, and Route 53 health-check failover gives the most fault tolerance, with promotion of the secondary when needed.

x.A: An EC2 FTP server storing to Glacier and a nightly job doesn't process files as soon as possible, and Glacier retrieval adds delay.
x.B: A nightly batch job from an EBS volume has the same delay and keeps a server to manage.
x.C: Transfer Family stores files in S3 or EFS, not on EBS volumes, so this design is wrong.
x.D: Transfer Family provides a managed FTP endpoint that stores files in S3 with no change for the FTP clients. An S3 event invokes Lambda for each file, and the function deletes the file after processing, within Lambda's 15 minute limit.

x.A: Databases on EC2 mean managing the servers, which increases operational overhead.
x.B: RDS is a managed database service that handles patching, backups, and failover, and encryption at rest protects the sensitive data. It increases security and reduces overhead.
x.C: Moving transactional data to S3 changes the data store, and Macie only discovers sensitive data rather than replacing a database.
x.D: CloudWatch Logs monitors logs and doesn't provide data security and protection for a database.

x.A: CloudFront doesn't support the TCP and UDP game traffic, and caching isn't useful for real-time multiplayer data.
x.B: ALBs support HTTP and HTTPS only, so they can't carry the UDP and general TCP game traffic.
x.C: Global Accelerator sends TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS global network to the closest healthy NLB endpoint, which reduces latency and improves performance. You define listeners for the ports.
x.D: API Gateway is for HTTP and WebSocket APIs and doesn't suit TCP and UDP game traffic.

x.A: A Lambda function URL gives the function a dedicated HTTPS endpoint with no extra services, so the third party can call it directly. It's the simplest option.
x.B: An ALB in front of Lambda adds a service to deploy and pay for, and it needs more setup.
x.C: An SNS topic doesn't have a public hostname to receive webhooks, so third parties can't call it like that.
x.D: An SQS queue doesn't have a public endpoint for a webhook to call in this way.

x.A: A wildcard custom domain name in a Route 53 hosted zone, pointing to the API Gateway endpoint, gives each customer an individual URL without a separate record or zone per customer.
x.B: The certificate must be in the same Region as a Regional API endpoint, so a certificate in a different Region doesn't work.
x.C: Creating a hosted zone per customer takes a lot of work and doesn't scale.
x.D: A wildcard certificate in ACM in the same Region secures all the customers' subdomains with a single certificate.
x.E: Creating separate API endpoints per customer multiplies management work.
x.F: A custom domain name in API Gateway that uses the ACM certificate lets the REST API be served on the customers' URLs.

x.A: Macie automatically detects PII in S3. An EventBridge rule can filter its SensitiveData findings and send them to an SNS topic, which notifies the security team.
x.B: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't discover PII in S3 objects.
x.C: The Macie part is right, but SQS isn't a notification service for people. It is a queue, so the security team wouldn't be notified.
x.D: GuardDuty doesn't detect PII, and SQS doesn't notify a team.

x.A: Transitioning to S3 Standard after 30 days does nothing when objects already start in Standard, and doesn't reduce cost for the backup period.
x.B: Logs stay in Standard for the 30 days of frequent analysis, then move to Standard-IA, which is cheaper for the 60 days of backup. They're deleted at 90 days. Highly available storage is kept.
x.C: Moving to Glacier after 30 days is cheap, but Glacier retrieval delays and fees aren't suited to the highly available requirement, and no frequent analysis is needed after 30 days. It also doesn't keep high availability the way Standard-IA does.
x.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which isn't highly available, and Glacier at 90 days is unnecessary when logs are deleted then.

x.A: Secrets Manager stores secrets, but it doesn't encrypt Kubernetes secrets inside the etcd store of the cluster.
x.B: Enabling EKS secrets encryption with a KMS key uses envelope encryption to encrypt Kubernetes secrets stored in etcd.
x.C: The EBS CSI driver is for persistent volumes and doesn't encrypt etcd secrets.
x.D: EBS default encryption encrypts volumes, not the Kubernetes secrets in etcd.

x.A: Scaling the production database doesn't separate the data scientists' queries from production, so complex queries could still affect it.
x.B: The standby in a Multi-AZ instance deployment can't be read from, so the data scientists can't use it.
x.C: Multi-AZ plus two read replicas means paying for more instances than needed.
x.D: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standby instances, which serve as highly available failover targets and also handle read queries through the reader endpoint. It's cost-effective with no extra replicas.

x.A: RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster across three AZs gives high availability and read scaling. ElastiCache for Redis with high availability stores session data and caches reads, and the Auto Scaling web tier across three AZs scales with traffic.
x.B: Memcached has no replication or failover, so it can't keep session data highly available.
x.C: Migrating from MySQL to DynamoDB needs major application changes, which isn't implied by the requirements.
x.D: A single-AZ database isn't highly available across the three AZs.

x.A: CloudFront geographic restrictions with an allow list let only viewers in specified countries access the content, which lets the company roll out country by country. A custom error message can be shown to others.
x.B: Signed URLs and cookies control who has access, not which country the viewer is in.
x.C: Encrypting the content doesn't restrict access by location.
x.D: Time-restricted signed URLs control when content is accessed, not where.

x.A: A multi-site active/active setup with SQL Server Enterprise and Always On needs expensive licensing and always-on infrastructure, so it doesn't minimize costs.
x.B: A warm standby RDS for SQL Server with DMS CDC costs more to run all the time than a pilot light, and DMS CDC may not hold an RPO of 30 seconds reliably.
x.C: Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates disk changes to AWS, so the RPO is seconds, and a pilot light keeps compute off until needed, so cost is low. The RTO of 60 minutes is achievable.
x.D: Nightly backups give an RPO of up to a day, not 30 seconds.

x.A: DMS to create instances in multiple Regions adds complexity and doesn't give a built-in reader for reporting.
x.B: Single-AZ isn't highly available, and a read replica in the same zone doesn't improve availability.
x.C: An RDS Multi-AZ cluster deployment gives high availability and has readable standby instances, so reporting can use the reader endpoint. It's managed and needs little effort. It also fits the requirement of staying on Oracle.
x.D: A Multi-AZ instance deployment is an RDS option and doesn't create an Aurora database, because Aurora is a separate engine.

x.A: Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB are serverless, so you pay only when requests come in, which fits unpredictable and idle periods cheaply.
x.B: ECS behind an ALB with RDS runs continuously, so it costs more during idle times.
x.C: A Cognito user pool handles sign-up and sign-in for the customers who paid, with no servers.
x.D: An identity pool gives AWS credentials to users, but it doesn't authenticate users itself the way a user pool does.
x.E: Amplify serves the frontend with an integrated CloudFront setup, which is low cost with no servers.
x.F: S3 static hosting can't run PHP, because it serves only static files.

x.A: S3 signed cookies don't exist. CloudFront signed cookies are the equivalent, and they're better for multiple files rather than a single rental.
x.B: CloudFront signed URLs give time-limited access to a specific file, which suits on-demand content like a movie rental or a music download for premium customers.
x.C: Origin access control only limits direct access to S3 so content goes through CloudFront. It doesn't separate premium from other customers.
x.D: Field-level encryption protects sensitive form data and doesn't block access to media.

x.A: Turning on discount sharing in the management account's billing preferences lets Savings Plan benefits apply across accounts in the organization.
x.B: Discount sharing is controlled from the management account, not from the account that bought the plan.
x.C: Savings Plans aren't shared through Resource Access Manager. Discount sharing handles it.
x.D: Sharing requires accounts to be in the same organization. Creating a new payer account in this way is unnecessary and doesn't preserve the existing plan.
x.E: The accounts have to be consolidated into an organization for sharing to apply. Creating the organization from the account that has the plan and inviting the others makes it the management account and enables sharing.

x.A: A canary release deployment sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version so it can be verified with minimal customer impact, and then it's promoted to production. No data is lost and customers keep the same endpoint.
x.B: Importing in merge mode into the production API can change it directly without a gradual rollout, and merge mode can leave old definitions in place.
x.C: Overwrite mode replaces the whole API and deploys straight to production without a gradual test, so customers could be affected.
x.D: A new API and custom domain with a DNS switch causes a full cutover, so any problem hits all customers, and DNS caching delays things.

x.A: Latency routing sends users to the lowest latency endpoint, not to an error page when the site is down.
x.B: A Route 53 active-passive failover with a health check on the ALB sends traffic to a static error page in S3 only when the ALB is unhealthy. It's simple and needs no servers.
x.C: An EC2 instance hosting the error page is extra infrastructure to run, and this isn't an active-active use case.
x.D: Multivalue answer routing returns multiple healthy values and doesn't act as a failover to an error page.

x.A: Storage Gateway's NFS interface is for file gateway, which doesn't work with tape-based backup applications.
x.B: EFS can't be mounted by the on-premises backup applications for tape replacement without extra connectivity, and it isn't a tape replacement.
x.C: EFS doesn't support iSCSI.
x.D: Tape Gateway presents an iSCSI virtual tape library, so the existing backup applications and workflows keep working while the physical tapes are replaced by virtual tapes stored in S3 and Glacier.

x.A: Kinesis Data Firehose ingests high-volume streaming data in near real time and delivers it directly to S3 with no servers or code to manage.
x.B: Glue is an ETL and analytics service, not an ingestion service for streaming from sensors.
x.C: Lambda would need code and the ingestion layer to be built, which adds overhead.
x.D: DMS migrates databases and isn't designed to ingest streaming sensor data.

x.A: Systems Manager templates (documents) automate operations tasks and can't control which services an account can use.
x.B: OUs per department with SCPs attached restrict which AWS services each account can use. It's central and easy to manage.
x.C: CloudFormation provisions resources but doesn't prevent users from using other services.
x.D: Service Catalog lets users deploy approved products but doesn't block them from using other services directly.

x.A: A NAT instance has to be patched, scaled, and made highly available, so it adds operational overhead.
x.B: A NAT gateway in the public subnets gives the private subnet outbound internet access without allowing inbound connections. It's managed, so it adds no overhead and is secure.
x.C: An internet gateway route would make the private subnet public, and the database instances would be exposed to the internet.
x.D: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect connections to on-premises, not internet access.

x.A: A Lambda resource policy controls who can invoke the function, not whether it can use a KMS key.
x.B: The Lambda execution role needs kms:Decrypt permissions so the function can decrypt its environment variables.
x.C: The function policy is the same as the resource policy, which governs invocation, not KMS access.
x.D: The KMS key policy must also allow the Lambda execution role to use the key, because KMS requires access to be allowed in the key policy.
x.E: The key policy should name the execution role (the principal that uses the key), not the Lambda resource policy.
